International Journal of Educational Research 35 (2001) 651–674 Chapter 2 The persuasiveness of persuasive discourse Patricia A
Sperl Department of Human Development, University of Maryland, 3304 Benjamin Building, College Park, MD, 20742 1131, USA Abstract This investigation explored why and how persuasion occurs
Toward this end, we examined the processing of two articles under conditions called for in the persuasion and conceptual change literatures
One unique aspect of the current study was the use of topic-speciﬁc measures of beliefs, knowledge (i.e., perceived and demonstrated), and interest
Theperformance of members of three educational communities (i.e., undergraduates, graduate students, and faculty) was compared, as was the knowledge and interest of more or less persuaded readers
One article argued that there are prenatal similarities among humans andother mammals, while the second presented a favorable view of same-sex marriages
Although both articles produced signiﬁcant changes in readers’ beliefs, knowledge, and interest, there were performance differences by text, educational community, and persuasion group
Resultsshowed that readers’ perceptions of their knowledge played a more signiﬁcant role in persuasion outcomes than the knowledge they actually demonstrated
Outcomes suggest the need to look more closely at the relationship between knowledge and interest in subsequentstudies of persuasion

The goal of this research was to extend current understanding of the conditions, which foster changes in readers’ knowledge and beliefs about contestable issues.Most individuals have encountered some written or verbal message that hasmarkedly altered their views or deeply touched their emotions
Such a message mayhave stimulated their thinking in surprising and unexpected ways
It may havestrengthened their position or resolve on a given topic, caused them to react withanger or disbelief, or led them to see some sensitive or controversial subject in a positive light
The message may even have been powerful enough to provoke them to act or to shift their perspective on the stated issues
That is to say, they may havefound themselves persuaded (Miller, 1980; Stiff, 1994)
Why and how persuasion occurs is an entirely different matter.Indeed, such questions have been the catalyst for centuries of philosophical debate and psychological inquiry
A fascination with persuasion reaches deep into human history, as evidenced by the dialogues of Plato (Carey, 1994) and the treatises of Aristotle (Cooper, 1932)
Inancient times, oration was the art of verbal persuasion, and Plato, in his dialogues,raised doubts about the divinity of oration
In effect, Plato was among the ﬁrst toclaim that oration, as a persuasive art, could be learned

Aristotle, Plato’s pupil,forwarded one of the earliest models of persuasion, declaring that the keys topersuasion lie in the ethos (i.e., objective characteristics) of the author, the pathos (i.e., subjectivity or emotionalism) of the listener, and in the arguments themselves

Even though current theories and models of persuasion and conceptual change havebecome increasingly more elaborate and sophisticated, they still pay homage to theideas forwarded by Plato and Aristotle

For instance, rhetoricians and philosophers stress how aspects of the message can stimulate or stiﬂe the persuasion process (Chambliss, 1994, 1995; Toulmin, 1958).Therefore, in judging the persuasiveness of a message, they inquire whether theauthor’s premises are clearly stated, the arguments and counter-arguments well developed, and whether the author evokes the emotions of the audience

Similarly, social psychologists frequently explore how various aspects of the source, message,recipient, and media inﬂuence attitude change (Hovland, Janis, & Kelley, 1953;Jaccard, 1981; Johnson, 1994)
Such researchers ask whether the reader or listenerﬁnds the author credible, has experiences relative to the topic, or can make sense ofthe message
As with others (Dole & Sinatra, 1994, 1999; Petty & Cacioppo, 1981,1986), we hold that persuasion represents a conﬂuence of such person and messagefactors

That is, while characteristics of the person and the message can be statistically isolated and analyzed, it is truly their interplay that affords the greatest understanding as to why and how persuasion occurs

Various models of persuasion (e.g., Elaboration Likelihood Model or ELM; Petty & Cacioppo, 1986) and conceptual change (e.g., Cognitive Reconstruction ofKnowledge Model or CRKM; Dole & Sinatra, 1998) acknowledge that changes inattitude or conceptual understanding occur as a result of the interaction of personand text
For example, the ELM, the best known and most tested model ofpersuasion (Stiff, 1994), proposes that a persuasive message can be processed through one of two routes, the central or the peripheral
The central processing route is pursued when there is thoughtful consideration of a message or its arguments
Thisroute is presumed to produce changes in schematic structures, thereby resulting inenduring shifts in attitude

In contrast, peripheral processing results from attentionto simple cues contained in the persuasive message or context (e.g., page length).Thus, this processing route can result in relatively temporary attitude changes
The speciﬁc route pursued and the degree to which this path results in a marked change of attitude depends on several factors
For example, the quality of the stated arguments (i.e., strong and weak) affect individuals’ responses to the message
For instance, an overly hot room or a particularly long reading can spark attitude change because these qualities triggerrather primitive affective states

From the central processing route, elaborations (i.e., the scrutiny of the stated arguments) also inﬂuence persuasion and are a consequence of individuals’ motivation and their ability to process the message

Similarly, the CRKM describes learner (e.g., existing conceptions or motivation) and text (e.g., comprehensibility or coherence) conditions that result in therestructuring of conceptual knowledge by eliciting learner engagement
The CRKM posits three qualities ashighly predictive of conceptual change: strength of existing conceptions, conceptualcoherence, and individuals’ commitment or need to believe
Another learner variable speciﬁed in this model is the construct of motivation or a person’s desire to process new concepts

The CRKM, like the ELM, proposes that motivation encompassespersonal responsibility and a ‘‘need for cognition,’’ as well as conceptualdissatisfaction (Chinn & Brewer, 1993; West & Pines, 1985) and the social context(Guzzetti & Hynd, 1998)

Conditions central to learning and development Even though the ELM and CRKM address the interplay of person and text factors, these models do not address some of the fundamental conditions that we (e.g., Alexander, 1998; Murphy & Woods, 1996) and others (e.g., Pintrich, 1994)have identiﬁed as central to learning and development

In particular, our concernscenter on: *the speciﬁcity of the constructs identiﬁed in these models; *the potential for interplay among person variables; *the inﬂuence of processing non-contrived, controversial texts; *intra-individual response patterns; and *the impact of respondents’ educational backgrounds

Construct speciﬁcity In our research, we have determined that a focus on very broad variables, such as those indicated in the ELM and CRKM (e.g., prior knowledge and motivation), can mask signiﬁcant effects in learning and development (Alexander, Jetton, & Kulikowich, 1995; Alexander, Kulikowich, & Schulze, 1994; Alexander & Murphy,1998)
In fact, Dole and Sinatra (1998) explicitly note that there are multiple forms ofknowledge that need to be considered in conceptual change

Thus, in the currentstudy, the general construct of prior knowledge was replaced with two more speciﬁcknowledge forms ,perceived (i.e., self-reported) knowledge and demonstrated (i.e., tested) knowledge
The decision to compare ﬁndings for both perceived and demonstrated knowledge was sparked by the intriguing results from an earlier study (Murphy, 1998).P.A

Speciﬁcally, using both self-report and open-ended measures of knowledge, Murphy found that readers’ perceptions of their knowledge were more powerful predictors ofpersuasion than the knowledge they actually demonstrated
For that reason, similar self-report and open-ended measures were used in the current study

Like the term prior knowledge , motivation encompasses a plethora of important, related constructs in the literature (Murphy & Alexander, 2000; Pintrich, 1994).Because persuasion entails the response to a particular message forwarding speciﬁc arguments about a certain topic, we think topic-speciﬁc interest inﬂuences this change process
By topic-speciﬁc interest, we mean the level of interest thatindividuals report for a particular subject, such as the legalization of same-sexmarriages
Interest is mentioned in both the ELM and the CRKM, but as a dimension of motivation dealing with general relevance
Further, in these models, higher levels of interest translate into greater changes in attitudes or conceptualunderstanding
Yet, our own research would suggest a less linear relationshipbetween topic interest and persuasion, a point elaborated in the subsequent sectionon interplay (Murphy & Alexander, 2001)

Interplay of person variables In their model, Petty and Cacioppo (1986) state that higher levels of prior knowledge can translate into biased processing of textual arguments, thus negativelyaffecting persuasion
The results from our exploratory study of persuasion supportthis knowledge pattern (Alexander, Murphy, Buehl, & Sperl, 1998)
Too little knowledgeappeared to result in peripheral processing or limited engagement of the text, and toomuch knowledge seemed to produce the type of biased processing the ELM andCRKM would predict

Because knowledge of the topic and interest in that topic have been inextricably intertwined in our research (e.g., Alexander & Dochy, 1995; Alexander & Murphy,1998), a similar threshold can be predicted for interest as for knowledge
That is,when interest in the topic is too low there is superﬁcial or limited processing of thecontroversial message
When interest in the topic is very high, however, we wouldassume that the individuals might come to that message with biases that restrict theirability to beneﬁt from the authors’ arguments

Naturally occurring texts and controversial issues Much of the research on persuasion centers on discourse expressly crafted to highlight particular textual features or elements, such as the argument structure orcohesion
As a result, these numerous investigations and the predictions theyinstigate may not generalize to the unmodiﬁed discourse found in individuals’everyday environments
For example, in a number of studies, textual materials wereeither ‘‘fabricated’’ (Slusher & Anderson, 1996,p
113) or crafted from one source(e.g., an article from Science; Kardash & Scholes, 1995) or multiple sources (e.g., newspapers and public health information; Kardash & Scholes, 1996)
the case of the ELM (Petty & Cacioppo, 1986), most of the authors’ studies employed short texts, one or two paragraphs in length
In addition, the experimentalmaterials were often contrived by the researchers to highlight the argument structure
Petty and Cacioppo (1986) explicitly state that it would be difﬁcult to assess persuasion under more natural conditions, as with the reading of unmodiﬁed oruncontrived texts
Yet, reading naturalistic, persuasive texts is one aspect ofecological validity expressly called for in the literature (Bronfenbrenner, 1989;Chambliss & Garner, 1996)

Consequently, naturally occurring texts were used inthis study rather than messages contrived or modiﬁed for experimental purposes.The phrase naturally occurring refers to persuasive materials that likely exist in individuals’ environments (e.g., newspaper editorials, magazine articles, or pamph- lets) and which are presented to readers without modiﬁcation
In this study,participants read two articles from Life in their entirety and directly from the magazine
The use of non-contrived texts afforded us the opportunity to extend thecurrent research on persuasion that has relied heavy on specially constructed texts
Beyond this issue of contrived versus naturally occurring texts, the role that the underlying topic played in the persuasive process was also of interest
In thisinvestigation, participants read controversial texts about prenatal differences between humans and other mammals, and about the legalization of same-sex marriages
Although other researchers have targeted controversial subjects, theyhave not always viewed persuasion as a shift in general stance relative to acontentious idea
Instead, they have focused on changes in readers’ understanding ofparticular and veriﬁable content associated with that topic

For example, Kardash and Scholes (1995, 1996) and Slusher and Anderson (1996) examined belief change about AIDS by gauging readers’ positions on a series ofveriﬁable statements, such as the idea that AIDS can be transmitted by casual contact or by mosquito bites
They described individuals’ views on these statements prior to and following their reading of informational text as either ‘‘accurate’’ or‘‘inaccurate’’ beliefs

Even though we agree that the accuracy and inaccuracy ofindividuals’ notions can be important aspects of the persuasion process, we wouldplace these more factual understandings under the heading of knowledge in the current investigation

A more encompassing orientation toward a controversial topicwould be indicative of individuals’ beliefs (e.g., same sex marriages should orshould notbe legalized)—an orientation that is not simply a reﬂection of the depth or accuracy of knowledge (Chinn & Brewer, 1993)
Intra-individual explorations Although empirical research on persuasion and conceptual change has been extensive, explorations of intra-individual differences have been relatively rare
Most often, in theliterature, ﬁndings regarding the persuasion process are based on a single text and,thus, a single topic
Under such conditions, the question of generalizability of ﬁndings cannot be adequately addressed
patterns across situations, each participant in this study was asked to read and respond to two controversial articles
Participants’ beliefs, knowledge, and interestsrelative to those articles were measured both prior to and following reading
In this way, we hoped to increase the generalizability of our ﬁndings
Along with intelligence, Petty and Cacioppo (1986) identify educational level as an important aspect of the ability to process
However, they go on to state that becauseof the sparse literature on the role of educational level, they could not consider thisvariable in any detailed way in the ELM

We have found it invaluable to exploreknowledge and beliefs from the standpoint of participants’ educational level (e.g.,Alexander & Dochy, 1995; Alexander, Murphy, Guan, & Murphy, 1998; Alexander,Murphy, & Woods, 1997 ).In these studies, we ascertained that individuals in varying educational communities (e.g., high school students, undergraduates, and experts) displayed distinct patterns of beliefs, knowledge, and interests relative to anarray of topics
However, we had not considered how the distinctions among theseeducational communities might inﬂuence the processing of controversial texts

Based on the aforementioned issues, the following questions guided this study: *What changes occur in participants’ beliefs, perceived knowledge, demonstratedknowledge, and topic-speciﬁc interests as a consequence of reading texts thatforward a particular view on a controversial topic
*In what ways do mature readers respond differentially to two naturally occurringtexts that present certain views on controversial topics
*How does the educational level of mature readers inﬂuence the nature and degreeto which they are persuaded by written text
*How do the proﬁles of those who are more persuaded by their reading ofcontroversial texts differ from the proﬁles of those who are less persuaded
Method As noted, participants in this study represented three educational communities— undergraduate students, graduate students, and faculty
Speciﬁcally, participantsincluded 37 undergraduate students, 25 graduate students, and 20 faculty from alarge, urban, land-grant university in the eastern United States
The 37 under-graduates, mostly juniors and seniors, were enrolled in an upper level educationalpsychology course

These undergraduates were ethnically diverse (approximately 51% Caucasian, 19% African American, 14% Hispanic, 8% Asian, and 8% mixed or unspeciﬁed) and represented a variety of majors (e.g., psychology, criminal justice,physical education, and business)
The breakdown of females and males wasrelatively consistent with undergraduate education courses with 26 females (70.3%)and 11 males (29.7%)
Twenty-ﬁve masters and doctoral students from the same institution also took part in this study
Most of these individuals were pursuing degrees in humandevelopment, although other majors (e.g., counseling and student services) were represented
The breakdown of females and males was 20 (80%) and 5 (20%),P.A
Twenty faculty members from colleges of education also volunteered to be participants in this investigation
Faculty who took part in the study are nationally recognized experts in human development, educational psychology, special educa-tion, teacher education, measurement and statistics, and literacy
There were 11 females (55%) and 9males (45%) among the faculty respondents
Texts For the experimental texts, two articles were selected from the same issue of Life magazine

Prior research had shown such professionally crafted articles to besuitable in length, reading difﬁculty, and appeal for our targeted communities(Buehl, Alexander, Murphy, & Sperl, 2001; Murphy & Alexander, 2001)
Thesearticles were two-sided refutational texts, which means that the authors present bothsides of the issue although one side is more strongly and positively supported whilethe other is rebutted
One of the articles, What does it mean to be one of us
(Miller, 1996), made the case for similarities in the embryos and fetuses of humans and other animals (e.g., chickens, pigs, and chimpanzees)

This article, referred to as thePrenatal Similarities text, consisted of 15 pages and 2955 words, and incorporated acaptivating display of 25 photographs to support its contention of similarities, alongwith extensive factual information
The second article, When we talk about gay marriage, what do we really mean
(Ferrato, Dowling, & Nyary, 1996), took a favorable stance on the legalization ofsame-sex marriages
This article, referred to as the Same-Sex Marriage text, was 8 pages long and contained 1171 words and 8 photographs

Unlike the Prenatal Similarities text, the Same-Sex Marriage text included limited factual content, relyinginstead on personal information about a gay couple trying to deal with the lack oflegal support for their non-traditional lifestyle
We believed that any attemptto copy these articles or remove them from the magazine would alter theirappearance and decrease the ecological validity of the study
Pre-reading response task Participants were asked a series of topic-speciﬁc questions before they read the articles

These questions provided information about respondents’ initial beliefsrelative to each article’s stated premise, their perceived knowledge, their demon-strated knowledge, and their interest in the topic
Topic beliefs Participants indicated their stance on a statement derived from the main premise of each article
participant indicated his or her position on the statement by placing anX on a line (150 mm) running from strongly disagree tostrongly agree
This variation of a Likert scale allows resulting data to be analyzed in a continuous rather than discrete manner
strongly strongly disagree agree Responses were recorded in millimeters, with higher numbers indicative of a stronger agreement with the authors’ premise
To decrease the effect for socialdesirability, the position statement for the Prenatal Similarities article was worded counter to the actual premise of the article

Speciﬁcally, we asked participants to indicate their view on the statement: ‘‘Before birth, humans are uniquely differentfrom all other forms of animal life.’’ Responses to this statement were reverse codedso that higher numbers signiﬁed greater agreement with the author’s actual claim(i.e., that there are great similarities prenatally between human embryos and fetusesand those of other animals)
Topic knowledge Participants’ knowledge of the article topics was gauged in two ways

First, their perceived knowledge was assessed by asking them ‘‘to indicate how much you think you know’’ about prenatal differences or the legalization of same-sex marriages on a continuum from relatively nothing toa great deal

Once again a 150 mm line was used for this assessment and scored it in a fashion similar to the previous two questions.Second, as a measure of demonstrated knowledge , participants were asked to share their knowledge about each topic

Speciﬁcally, prior to reading, participants wereasked: ‘‘What background information or knowledge helped you form your positionon this issue [prenatal differences or legalization of same-sex marriages]

In otherwords, tell us what you already know about this subject.’’ Participants’ responses were scored by marking and categorizing each information unit in their answers in a manner described in the section on coding and reliability
For this scoring, aninformation unit was operationally deﬁned as a complete and accurate thought,roughly equivalent to a phrase or independent clause
Topic interest In a similar fashion, participants indicated their interest in the article’s topic on a continuum from very disinterested tovery interested
Speciﬁcally, they were asked to indicate how interested they were in reading about prenatal similarities anddifferences between humans and other animals or about the legalization of same-sexmarriages
Responses were scored on the 150 mm line in a manner identical to the beliefs question.P.A
Post-reading response task Immediately after reading each article, participants responded to a set of questions similar to those included in the pre-reading task
The belief statement and the directions to respondents were identical to those at pre-reading
With regard to topic knowledge and interest assessments, variations of the pre-reading questions wereused

For example, for topic interest participants were asked to indicate ‘‘howinteresting you found this topic [prenatal differences or legalization of same-sexmarriages] to be.’’ Similarly, when marking their level of perceived knowledge,respondents were directed to ‘‘indicate how much you think you now know about’’prenatal differences between humans and other animals, or the legalization of same-sex marriages
This same approach to assessing readers’ beliefs, perceived knowledge, and interest had been used in a prior study (Buehl et al., 2001) with strong test-retestreliabilities (i.e., 0.74–0.97)

Finally, the question assessing participants’ demon-strated knowledge read as follows: ‘‘What speciﬁcally did you learn from reading thisarticle about [prenatal differences or legalization of same-sex marriages]
Coding and reliabilities Three doctoral students were taught the rubric for coding participants’ responses to the demonstrated knowledge question
Responses were codedbased on the number of information units offered by participants
Theseinformation units were basically statements containing factual information relatedto each article (e.g., ‘‘Hawaii is trying to legalize gay marriages’’)

Because of thedistinction in wording for the pre-reading and the post-reading demonstratedknowledge questions (i.e., ‘‘tell what you already know’’ versus ‘‘tell me what learnedfrom the article’’), these two items were scored differently
Speciﬁcally, pre-reading demonstrated knowledge was a simple total of all information units embodied in participants’ written responses to the pre-reading question

Post-reading demon-strated knowledge, in contrast, was the sum of any new information units containedin responses to the post-reading question plus the number of information units in thepre-reading task
Our decision to score demonstrated knowledge in this manner wasbased on the directive to participants to tell us what they learned from the readingthese articles
Information units were not the only content in participants’ written responses to the demonstrated knowledge question, however
Although not included in our ﬁnal analysis, we also noted contextual and evaluative statements

Contextual statementsconveyed information of a more personal nature, such as participants’ backgroundor experiences (e.g., ‘‘I went to Catholic school’’ or ‘‘I am gay’’), or they describedwhere or from whom they learned the information that they included in theirresponses (e.g., ‘‘I have gay friends who talk about this issue’’ or ‘‘The articlespeciﬁcally said that y’’)

Evaluative statements were marker clauses or phrases that indicated how the participant judged the nature or strength of the information that followed (e.g., ‘‘I don’t know much about the topic’’ or ‘‘It is my opinion that y’’).P.A
In training, the codings for several sample answers were discussed and prototypes of each response category were provided
Once they felt conﬁdent about theseresponse categories, the three coders independently scored the pre-reading and post- reading responses for 12 of the 82 participants (approximately 15%)
Interrater agreement (i.e., number of agreements divided by total number of information unitscategorized) was 0.93
All disagreements were resolved in conference with the ﬁrstauthor, who conducted the training
Results and discussions This study was designed to explore changes in readers’ beliefs, perceived knowledge, demonstrated knowledge, and interest after reading two naturallyoccurring persuasive texts
An additional purpose was to examine differences inreaders’ responses to the two texts
Participants expected to be persuaded toward theauthors’ premises regarding prenatal similarities and the legalization of same-sexmarriages after reading the articles
Signiﬁcant increases in readers’ perceivedknowledge, demonstrated knowledge, and interest were also anticipated
However,there was an expectation that the basis for the persuasiveness of the two articles would vary to some degree

For example, the author of the Prenatal Similarities article stressed factual information to forward his arguments, whereas a moreemotional response seemed more central to the persuasiveness of the Same-SexMarriage article
Thus, knowledge should undergo more change for the PrenatalSimilarities than for the Same-Sex Marriage article, resulting in a time by textinteraction for perceived or demonstrated knowledge

The means and standards deviations for participants’ beliefs, perceived knowl- edge, demonstrated knowledge, and interest indicate differences in responses to pre- reading and post-reading measures, as well as differences in responses to the Prenatal Similarities and Same-Sex Marriage articles (see Table 1)

To test the hypotheses,data were subjected to repeated measures multivariate analysis of variance(MANOVA) with beliefs, perceived knowledge, demonstrated knowledge, andinterest as dependent variables, and time and text as within-subject variables
If readers were persuaded by the texts and if their perceived knowledge, demonstrated knowledge, and interest changed accordingly, there would be a signiﬁcant effect for time
Further, if the paths to persuasion for the two articles differed, as hypothesized, there would be a text effect, as well as a time by textinteraction
There weresigniﬁcant main effects for time [ F(4, 78)=108.08, po0:001] and text [ F(4, 78)=2.58, po0:05]
The time by text interaction was also statistically signiﬁcant [F(4, 78)=5.44, po0:001]

The univariate ANOVAs revealed that the omnibus effect for time was attributable to changes in readers’ reported stances (i.e., beliefs) after reading the Prenatal Similarities and Same-Sex Marriage articles [ F(1,81)=56.8, po0:001 ;P.A
Readers’ perceived knowledge, demonstrated knowledge, and interest also signiﬁcantly increased after reading the two texts [ F(1,81)=21.74, po0:001 ;MSeo755 :23]

The time by text interaction was signiﬁcant for beliefs [ F(1,81)=15.81, po0:001 ; MSe ¼501 :87] and demonstrated knowledge [ F(1,81)=5.43, po0:05 ;MSe ¼5:61]

Educational community and persuasion The potential effects that undergraduate students’, graduate students’, and faculty’s experience and training might have on their interactions with persuasive texts were also explored

Means and standard deviations for these three educationalcommunities by text are presented in Table 2 It was hypothesized that theeducational community would play a more inﬂuential role in the processing of thePrenatal Similarities article than it would for the Same-Sex Marriage article, becausea number of faculty participants are nationally recognized experts in humandevelopment

On this basis, we expected that the knowledge and interests of facultywould be higher than the knowledge and interests of undergraduates and graduate students for the Prenatal Similarities article, especially at pre-reading
To test this expectation, the data for beliefs, perceived knowledge, demonstrated knowledge, andinterests for each article were subjected to the repeated measures MANOVA

Knowledge, interest, and belief differences by persuasion group The ﬁnal research question in this study pertained to the perceived knowledge, demonstrated knowledge, and reported interests of individuals who were more or less persuaded by what they read
As the basis of this analysis, persuasion groupswere formed using a two-step procedure
This resulted in the formation ofthree tentative persuasion groups (i.e., less, moderate, and more), using 712 SD in belief change (in the direction of the article’s premise) as our guide
The changescores for the Prenatal Similarities article ranged from –127 to 111, as compared to arange of –14 to 136 for the Same-Sex Marriage article
For example, groupmeans marked with the subscriptb are signiﬁcantly higher for a particular variable than those marked by the subscript a.P.A
They also suggest powerful, almost polar reactions some participants had to the author’s argument that human embryos and fetuses arestrikingly similar to those of other mammals
Second, to make these groupings more theoretically sound, we inspected a graphic representation of the distribution as a way to conﬁrm our natural clustering ofparticipants
This representation was used to move certain individuals from onecluster to another and, thus, ﬁnalize our persuasion groups
As a result of these steps,29 participants were placed in the less persuaded group, 32 in the moderate cluster,and 21 in the more persuaded group for the Prenatal Similarities article
For theSame-Sex Marriage article, 30 participants constituted the less persuaded group, 35in the moderate cluster, and 17 made up the more persuaded group

Analyses of variance conﬁrmed that these groups differed statistically on the basis of belief change for the Prenatal Similarities [ F(2,79)=80.12, po0:0001 ;MSe ¼534 :33] and the Same-Sex Marriage articles [ F(2,79)=40.74, po0:0001 ;MSe ¼222 :28]

Conclusions and implications The literature on persuasion and conceptual change has identiﬁed key person and text factors that instigate changes in those hearing or reading messages intended toevoke such change
The goal of this study was to extend that research by consideringconditions others have judged important but difﬁcult to assess in the persuasionprocess (Dole & Sinatra, 1998; Petty & Cacioppo, 1986)

These conditions includethe speciﬁcity of the constructs; the interplay among variables; the inﬂuence ofprocessing non-contrived, controversial texts; intra-individual response patterns; andthe impact of respondents’ educational backgrounds
The outcomes reported herein set the stage for subsequent studies of persuasion by shedding light on the person and text factors underlying changes in reader understanding and beliefs
Of course, the contributions of this study to the persuasion literature must be understood in terms of its potential limitations
First, the persuasion process wasinvestigated using naturally occurring texts, rather than materials expresslycontrived for experimental purposes

As a result, particular textual features thatmay have heightened the statistical comparability of our persuasive articles could notbe controlled, as other researchers have done (Kardash & Scholes, 1996)
Consequently, it was impossible to tease apart the relative effects of certain textualP.A
elements, such as topic, clarity of arguments, or author credibility, as has been done in prior studies (Chambliss, 1995; Slusher & Anderson, 1996)
Moreover, the sampleconsisted of mature readers who were members of three educational communities
Outcomes that may arise when participants are less competent readers or less educationally oriented remain to be seen

In addition, because much of our prior research has centered on knowledge, interest, and beliefs (e.g., Alexander et al., 1995; Alexander et al., 1998), those samecomponents were included in this study
It can be argued that other variables oralternative measures of the included variables might paint a different picture of thepersuasion process

However, the components targeted are elements of varioustheories and models of belief change (e.g., Dole & Sinatra, 1998; Murphy, 1998) and have been incorporated in empirical investigations of persuasion and conceptual change (e.g., Anderson & Sechler, 1986; Wood & Eagly, 1981)
What has not beenconsidered in this multifaceted study is any predisposition to argumentation, such asopen-mindedness or resistance, that may well exist (Stanovich & West, 1997)
Norwas any speciﬁc measure of emotional reaction to the article included (Murphy,1998)
Even inlight of these limitations, there are consequential outcomes from this study thatprovide clues as to why and how persuasion occurs

Particular measures of general constructs In forwarding their model of cognitive change, Dole and Sinatra (1998) state that one of the challenges for those concerned with persuasion and conceptual change isidentifying and assessing the impact that varying types of knowledge play in theseprocesses

This investigation included two forms of knowledge that on the surfaceappear rather similar, perceived knowledge (i.e., what one thinks one knows) anddemonstrated knowledge (i.e., the relevant knowledge one produces)

Our ﬁndings suggest that perceptions of knowledge, as with research on self-efﬁcacy (e.g., Zimmerman,Bandura, & Martinez-Pons, 1992), are more potent forces in how one approaches acontroversial topic than what one may actually know
It would also appear thatthose with expertise are more conservative in their judgments than others, perhapsbecause of their awareness of the breadth and depth of the domain
Further, evenwhen judgments of knowledge seem misguided, they pertain to one’s interest in thetopic

Somewhat tempered levels of perceived knowledge may, in effect, signal the ‘‘need to know,’’ that is so important to subsequent changes in attitudes (Cacioppo & Petty, 1982) and conceptual understanding (Dole & Sinatra, 1998)
Although perceived and demonstrated knowledge were expected to operate somewhat differently in the persuasion process, it was not assumed that theirrelationship would be statistically non-signiﬁcant
This anomaly can be attributed tothe fact that our experts, who demonstrated the most knowledge of both topics atpre-reading and post-reading, conservatively judged their knowledge base
Even inthe area of their research (i.e., human development), experts’ knowledge ratings were comparable to the ratings of undergraduates and graduate students

open-ended nature of our demonstrated knowledge task understandably captured only a very select portion of participants’ understanding, especially for the experts.For this reason, we are currently experimenting with a demonstrated knowledge measure that incorporates both open and closed questions, as a means of examining both the breadth and depth of participants’ demonstrated knowledge and itssubsequent relation to perceived knowledge
Interplay of person variables As models of change, the ELM and the CRKM consider how the variables of knowledge and interest contribute to shifts in attitude or conceptual understanding
However, the speciﬁc nature of the presumed relationship between knowledge and interest in these leading models was not ascertained
That is, it was not apparentwhether knowledge and interest should be strongly correlated or whether lower orhigher levels of interest would limit change

Although knowledge and interest weresigniﬁcantly correlated in this investigation, the clear association we have typicallyfound for these two variables in our research (e.g., Alexander et al., 1995) did notemerge here
This pattern can be attributed largely to the experts in this study who consistently had the highest means for demonstrated knowledge, but the lowest means for topic interest
Perceived knowledge and reported interest were far better aligned for theseexpert participants
Truly, the experts in this study offered a unique portrait of thepersuasion process, as compared to the undergraduates and graduate students whoparticipated
These experts remind us that stimulating the interest, enhancing theknowledge, and changing the beliefs of those who are immersed in a relevant ﬁeld isno easy undertaking (Petty & Cacioppo, 1986)

Our ﬁndings do indicate that theinterplay between knowledge and interest is quite complex and not as straightfor- ward as existing models may portray, especially when alternate forms of knowledge are considered
Nature of the controversial topic Models of persuasion and conceptual change do give credence to text factors as contributors to the change process
However, there is more to text than whetherarguments are well made or the writing is cohesive
There is also the nature of theissue being discussed and whether that issue may be more readily addressed via knowledge-based arguments or by playing to the readers’ emotions

Thus, when Kardash and Scholes (1995) focus on AIDS, and speciﬁcally on readers’ scientiﬁcmisconceptions regarding this dreadful disease (e.g., AIDS can be transmitted viamosquito bites or casual contact), they are potentially researching something quitedifferent from those who seek to convince their audience that AIDS is not a divineplague or retribution for ungodly behavior

Our interest in belief change in this investigation is more in keeping with the latter than the former in that we have posed controversial issues to mature readers for which obviously ‘‘correct’’ or ‘‘accurate’’ positions do not exist
